en: The strong liquor in the leather flasks,
They poured it into cups,
Offered it to one another.
Drinking liquor and panting,
Drinking fermented mare's milk and growing heated,
Their bones grew hot,
Sweat trickled from their brows:
'Uncle, elder Koshoi,
We agree to your words,' they said.
'Two reins and one lead-rope,
We have given to hero Manas,' they said.
'If he treats the people well,
We shall keep giving thanks.
If he treats the people badly,
On the coming Day of Resurrection,
We shall make him a black donkey.
Uncle, elder Koshoi,
What you say is right,' they said.
'Whoever does not obey your word,
His seven forefathers are infidels,' they said.
'Let the earth swallow him,' they said.
'We agree to what you said,' they said.
'Two reins and one lead-rope,
We have given to hero Manas,' they said.
'Of slaughterer Lord Manas,
If we cannot obey his words,
If we ourselves turn our necks away,
May our eyes go blind!
Of blue-maned Lord Manas,
If we do not obey his fitting words,
If we do not go where he drives us,
The wretch who knows no master,
The wicked one who will not obey,
Whoever acts wickedly,
May the hairy-breasted earth strike him!
May the open-topped sky strike him!
May Akkelte's bullet strike him!
May the white matchcord's ember strike him!'
Saying this, the Muslims
Stood in rows, bursting with emotion,
Clamoring, they pronounced the curses.
Of any hero who would not obey,
'Let him simply die,' they said.
They chewed white-wheat flour,
They held the holy Quran.
'We agree, we agree, we agree!' they said.
'Two reins and one lead-rope,
We have given to hero Manas,' they said.
Taking knives in their hands,
Cutting off a twig,
They slit open a white-gray mare.
All the various khans,
Their arms up to the upper arm,
Dipped their hands in blood.
'This is what has been said,' they said.
'The words are settled,' they said.
Their elder uncle Koshoi,
Was satisfied then,
As were all the Muslims.
They now gathered together.
Upon a carpet with golden flowers,
Magnanimous Lord Manas,
They brought and placed him there.
When Manas sat upon the carpet,
With old Kyrgyl as their leader,
As though stricken by slaughter,
All the forty companions,
Their knees bending,
The magnanimous hero then,
To his uncle Koshoi,
They brought him at a run.
Did you see the forty companions?
Leopard Lord Manas,
Making his name known to the people,
A golden throne the size of a camel—
They brought Manas
And seated him upon it.
Placing him on a carpet, the forty companions
Now brought the slaughterer.
The hero who had been brought,
Your uncle Koshoi now saw:
'We have seen, we have seen, we have seen!' he said.
'Two reins and one lead-rope,
We have now given to you,' he said.
The edge of that carpet,
Koshoi grasped with his great hands.
Your elder uncle Koshoi,
He grasped that carpet,
And all the eight khans.
As though to obey his words,
As though to allot an inheritance,
The carpet lying before them,
All the eight khans
Now took it from every side.
The magnanimous hero then,
The people on the open steppe
Now raised him as khan.
They now agreed to his words.
Alöökö's countless wealth,
To all who had come,
He divided it, measuring with a whip.
All who had the means,
Taking many separate gold coins,
The gold coins allotted as booty,
They put them in their saddlebags,
Loaded them on their gelded camels.
'This is Khan Manas,' they said.
'This is the time he brings delight,' they said.
All who had gone now returned.
'The youngest of six lions,
God's beloved mortal,
May the magnanimous lion live safe,' they said,
Giving great thanks.
He made their felt walls rich with fat.
The khans he encountered,
He made them too rich to stand.
He made their lattice walls rich with fat.
The khans he met,
He gave them unfailing wealth.
Magnanimous Manas, the sultan,
They regarded him as Ala-Too.
The wealth Manas had won,
All who had gone
Returned unable to fit it all in.
The forty companions he led,
Hearing words from those who came:
'In the lowlands of a day's journey of steppe,
Along Chong-Koton,
Of the seven plains of Zherken,
Dwelling at their farthest reach,
Whom no mortal defeated in mounted wrestling,
His land hot, a terrible desert,
No man came there in rash excitement,
Heroes could not bend him down,
No one set foot there.
There was the famous Khan Shooruk.
His fame spread far,
Men stood helpless, unable to overcome him.
His world was in perfect balance,
Those who went fell short.
His land is a hot desert, they say.
What mortal dwelt there?
The people who fought there
Did not return.
Those who went and encountered it,
The heat burns and kills them, they say.
A water ewer set in the sand
Rumbles and boils, they say.
If it stays a meal-cooking's time,
Not a spoonful of water remains, they say.
Where no wild duck has flown,
It is a desert of red haze, they say.
He himself is an Indian Chinese—
No man goes to face him, they say.
Renowned Shooruk, they say,
Going straight to face him,
No mortal wages battle, they say.
If we fought and took Shooruk,
If you wished it, they say,
Of that people of fierce wrath,
Their women and girls are beautiful, they say.
Their women formidable, their men dogs,
In their waters lies dire peril.
Their females are most beautiful,
Their clear eyes shine, they say.
Of the person who beholds them,
Not a sliver of his soul remains, they say.
Khan Shooruk became an immeasurable hero.
His army numbered six multitudes,
Any mortal who went was killed.
Raging from that place,
He waged fierce fighting, they say.
The city of broad Kashkar,
Making its women and girls cry out,
He raided it six times, they say.
Breaking rock and making roads,
Such was Shooruk's fame;
He attacked many lands.
He won abundant wealth, they say.
The Noygut of broad Alay,
Taking their women and girls as spoil,
He raided them thoroughly, they say.
His army rides camels, they say,
At the word of an enemy they mount,
And all ride abreast, they say.
Riding camels and taking up spears,
What men are these who strike down upon your heads?
Against that Khan Shooruk
Let us go and launch a campaign.
Upon that khan's city
Let us bring fierce battle;
His camel-mounted troops
Let us conquer, leaving none.
Let us bind his warriors,
Let us slay his champions.
Taking gold coins loaded on elephants,
Taking a thousand palace maidens,
Let us wage measureless combat;
Let us take the measure of his people,
Let us settle their account beyond measure.
Khan Shooruk has gone mad;
Let us slaughter his court,
Bind his champions and return,
Let us turn their faces toward us.
While Akkula is safe,
While magnanimous Manas is here,
Where winged steeds have not trampled,
Let no land remain intact;
Where warriors have not thrust their spears,
Let no people remain intact.
Those who heed our words,
Let us hold them, teaching obedience;
Those who will not heed,
Let us subdue by force.
Making a road along the ridges,
Khan Shooruk is Chinese;
Let us find the way along the slopes,
Raising piercing cries and a clamor,
Let us charge in a mass.
Let us shatter and ravage his borders,
Let us take his abundant livestock;
Shooruk's girls and women
Let us take as booty.
With no enemy to clash with,
He entered straight and vented his fury, they say.
Making the Noygut tremble,
He raided them to their very roots, they say.
He drove away many of them;
The Noygut's abundant livestock,
Your father's grave, that Shooruk
Took away as booty.
There is no remedy for fate, he said;
I have much to say
To you, my lion Manas, he said.
If death has come, let us die;
If there is a way, with Shooruk
Let us try our strength in combat.
Let us bring hell upon his host;
Shooruk's many girls
Let us take as booty.
Red-dressed, crescent-waisted,
Of the swaying beauty
Let us drink our fill of delight.
As he was telling half
Let us find in a faithful spouse.”
His noble elder Bakay,
Warrior Manas's confidant,
Sharing death, united in life,
Blood-stained Manas's companion,
Your khan and elder Bakay said this;
Desire seized him from the unseen,
To your elder, leopard Bakay,
These words came unawares.
Lord Bakay, the protecting spirit,
Your saint, Manas's companion,
His companion who went scouting,
